source_title: New Fragment #3:4-5, lines 24-36, as quoted by Stuart George Hall in 'Melito of Sardis: On Pascha and Fragments' (2012 revised edition), pp. 62-96

author: Methodius of Olympus
quote: For we believe that, together with the Son, who was made man for our sakes, according to the good pleasure of His will, was also present the Father, who is inseparable from Him as to His divine nature, and also the Spirit, who is of one and the same essence with Him. For, as says Paul, the interpreter of the divine oracle, "God was in Christ reconciling the world unto Himself, not imputing their trespasses unto them." He thus shows that the Father was in the Son, because that one and the same will worked in them.
source_title: Methodius Oration Concerning Simeon and Anna

author: Methodius of Olympus
quote: For the mountains are to be explained by the heavens, and the ninety and nine sheep by the principalities and powers

author: Methodius of Olympus
quote: ...as though those who were baptized into Christ had been made Christs by communication of the Spirit, the Church contributing here their clearness and transformation into the image of the Word. And Paul confirms this, teaching it plainly, where he says: "For this cause I bow my knees unto the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, of whom the whole family in heaven and earth is named, that He would grant you, according to the riches of His glory, to be strengthened with might by His Spirit in the inner man; that Christ may dwell in your hearts by faith." For it is necessary that the word of truth should be imprinted and stamped upon the souls of the regenerate.

author: Methodius of Olympus
quote: ...the Word, leaving His Father in heaven, came down to be "joined to His wife;" and slept in the trance of His passion, and willingly suffered death for her, that He might present the Church to Himself glorious and blameless, having cleansed her by the laver, for the receiving of the spiritual and blessed seed, which is sown by Him who with whispers implants it in the depths of the mind; and is conceived and formed by the Church, as by a woman, so as to give birth and nourishment to virtue.

author: Methodius of Olympus
quote:
Chapter I.-Passages of Holy Scripture Compared.
For this cause shall a man leave his father and mother, and shall be joined unto his wife, and they two shall be one flesh. This is a great mystery: but I speak concerning Christ and the Church."

author: Methodius of Olympus
quote: For thus will it be most certainly agreed that the Church is formed out of His bones and flesh; and it was for this cause that the Word, leaving His Father in heaven, came down to be "joined to His wife; "

author: Methodius of Olympus
quote: Yet, while everything else seems rightly spoken, one thing, my friend, distresses and troubles me, considering that that wise and most spiritual man-I mean Paul-would not vainly refer to Christ and the Church the union of the first man and woman,

author: Methodius of Olympus
quote: The apostle's aim was not amiss when he compared the first condition of Adam with that of Christ. It is a perfectly accurate analogy: the church is generated from Adam's bones and flesh. For her sake the Word left his Father in heaven. He came down to be bonded with this woman, the church. Then he fell into the sleep of his passion. He willingly died for her.… He did this to make her ready for the blessed seed which he himself sows secretly in her, which she cherishes in the depth of her soul. The seed is sown that the church might receive it and fashion it like a woman, to bring forth and foster excellence.

author: Methodius of Olympus
quote:
For being made after the image of the Only-begotten, as I said, it has an unsurpassable beauty, and therefore evil spirits.
"for we wrestle not against flesh and blood; "

author: Methodius of Olympus
quote: Above all, taking the shield of faith, wherewith ye shall be able to quench all the fiery darts of the wicked. And take the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the spirit, which is the Word of God"
source_title: Methodius From the Discourse on the Resurrection

author: Methodius of Olympus
quote: Do not, therefore, lose courage on account of the schemes and slanders of the beast, but bravely prepare for the battle, armed with the helmet of salvation,

author: Odes of Solomon
quote:
Sheol saw me and was shattered, and Death ejected me and many with me.
I have been vinegar and bitterness to it, and I went down with it as far as its depth.
Then the feet and the head it released, because it was not able to endure my face.
And I made a congregation of living among his dead; and I spoke with them by living lips; in order that my word may not be unprofitable.
And those who had died ran towards me; and they cried out and said, Son of God, have pity on us.
And deal with us according to Your kindness, and bring us out from the bonds of darkness.
And open for us the door by which we may come out to You; for we perceive that our death does not touch You.
May we also be saved with You, because You are our Savior.
Then I heard their voice, and placed their faith in my heart.
And I placed my name upon their head, because they are free and they are mine.

author: Oecumenius
quote:
Therefore he said, "When he ascended on high." And that the gift is Christ's grace, and he himself gave it out, listen to David: "And when he ascended on high," he says, "Your magnificence was raised above the heavens." Whom did he lead captive? Us, of course, a beautiful and useful captivity. For when he had defeated the devil in the spiritual battle, he took us captive, not to subject us to slavery (for how could he have done this when we were already slaves?), but to free us from the bitter tyranny of that wicked one. But some have understood this from the cross, that when he ascended on the cross, he led captivity captive. He did indeed lead the devil captive, but in place of punishment he gave gifts and grace to those who had been captive...

But what does 'he ascended' mean? It is not necessary, he says, for the prophet to say 'he ascended' unless he knew that he had first descended. For someone usually says 'he ascended' about the one who had previously descended. For he who ascends or in what he ascends begins at the lower place so that he may be in the higher place, just as when someone begins to ascend, although he was not previously in a higher place.

Either he does not now begin his ascent, but he was indeed in a higher place from the beginning. But since he descended from there, he now ascends again. Therefore, where it says, "When he ascended," it is to be understood how it should be interpreted: "When he ascended," not as if he had just begun to ascend now, for he was from the beginning in the sublimity of divine dignity and paternal glory. But because, by his own dispensation and descent even to the lower parts, he ascended again for the appropriate manifestation of divine sublimity, it is said, "he ascended."

"Into the lowest parts of the earth." After which, it is evident that there are no lower parts. But he speaks of hell, looking at it as a common way of speaking, for this is how we are accustomed to say. Therefore, Jacob also says, "And you shall bring down my gray hairs with sorrow to hell." And David, "And I shall be likened to those who descend into the pit." For he called death the lower parts of the earth. "The same who also ascended." This refutes the blasphemy of Nestorius. For there is one who descended and who also ascended.
source_title: Commentary on the Epistle to the Ephesians, IV, 7-13

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
If the preposition through indicates a subservient role (as we examined at greater length when expounding the words "all things came into being through him", where we also set down the objections that appeared to us on this point), we must inquire how Paul is an apostle of Christ Jesus not from the will of God but through the will of God.

Now one person will say that Paul does not everywhere observe with strict precision the proper force of the prepositions, which is something he does in the case of other significations as well. But another, knowing the difference between 'through God' and through the will of God, will say that it would have been strange had it been written Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus through God; but if the will of God is subservient, God himself who uses it being the one who leads, this would not be unreasonable.

You will also give attention, concerning the will of God, to whether it can be predicated of Christ; so that, just as there is a "power" of God and a "wisdom" of God, so there may also be a will of him, having him as God's own subsistence; but if to anyone it seems out of place to say that the will of God is given substance, let him consider whether the apparent incongruity is not much the same also in the case of the "power" of God and the "wisdom" of God and the "word" of God, and the "truth" and the "resurrection" and the "way"; for it seems to me to hold much the same regarding all of these, as being given substance in the only-begotten Word.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Only in the case of the Ephesians did we find set down the phrase to the saints who are; and we inquire whether the addition of who are to the saints is not superfluous, and what it can signify. Consider, then, whether — just as in Exodus he who gives the oracle to Moses says that his own name is "the one who is" — so those who partake of the One who Is come to be beings, being called, as it were, from not being into being. For God chose the "things that are not", says this same Paul, "that he might bring to nothing the things that are". And someone will inquire how he brings to nothing the things that are; but let us hear him adding "so that no flesh may boast before God". For if anyone who has partaken of being, forgetting his participation, grants to himself the cause of his being, and does not refer all thanksgiving to the one who out of not being graciously granted him being "in his likeness" and "according to his image", then that which is is brought to nothing.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: All their error, therefore, has crept in from the reading of the prophets, which they do not understand — among which is that passage in Isaiah: "my chosen ones will not have children for a curse", and in Deuteronomy among the blessings: "blessed are the children of your womb" — and they suppose that these things are to be in the resurrection, not understanding that spiritual blessings were foretold. For Paul, "the vessel of election", interpreting spiritually all these blessings that are set down in the law, and knowing that they are not carnal, speaks to the Ephesians: "blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us with every spiritual blessing". And so all these blessings will be spiritual, when, rising from the dead, we attain eternal blessedness.
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 39

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But that what we say may be beyond doubt, let us use the voice of the Apostle Paul himself, who, writing to the Ephesians concerning spiritual blessings, pronounces in this manner: "Blessed", he says, "be God, and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places in Christ". Since indeed he knew that some readers, reading about blessings, could slip into this, that they should think them bodily and earthly, he wished to open more evidently to them what is the nature of the divine blessings, or where it is to be sought, and therefore he says: "who has blessed us", he says, "with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places in Christ". But also this, which he added, "with every blessing", is not idle, but full of apostolic vehemence. For because he knew that there are many things to be fulfilled which are commanded in the law, and that in each single commandment its own contests exist, in which through each one whoever should conquer would deserve a blessing, therefore he said: "who has blessed us with every spiritual blessing", that he might show them both to be many and to be spiritual. But in this saying, in which he says, "with every spiritual blessing", this too can be understood: that, for instance, every just and perfect person may receive the blessings of Leviticus, of which the discourse is now, and may receive also those which are written in the book of Numbers, and also those which are contained in the book of Genesis—the blessings of Noah to Shem and Japheth, and the blessings of Isaac to Jacob, and likewise the blessings of Jacob to Joseph and to Ephraim and Manasseh, and after these to the twelve patriarchs. Since therefore many are the blessings set down in the divine Scriptures, which seem indeed to be directed to each one of the saints—for instance, to Shem or Japheth or Joseph—yet not, as it seems to some, are they so directed to those alone that another cannot share in them, therefore the Apostle named them "spiritual", so that whoever can be made in virtue and spirit, for instance, a Shem or Japheth or Joseph or Isaac or Jacob, just as John also was "in the spirit and power of Elijah", may himself also become a partaker of that blessing whose virtue and spirit he has borne.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
Someone will say that, on account of the blessings in Leviticus and Deuteronomy, and wherever else in Scripture such things are recorded, the spiritual blessing is spoken of by way of contrast with those; as though the God and Father of Jesus Christ blesses us not with a bodily blessing like those, but with a spiritual one. And the heterodox will indeed take it in this way, supposing that from such an interpretation they will also gain occasion to sever the Godhead.

But we, having shown that not even in the case of the blessings according to the law are the blessings given — if they be understood bodily — to those who are believed to have lived according to the law and soundly, said that those who have so assumed either make him who gave the blessings a liar, or hold that what was promised to those who lived as he commanded is not what is understood from the ready-to-hand interpretation. For it follows upon "the law is spiritual" that the blessings in it too are spiritual. But the prophets, for instance, did not obtain the blessings bodily; for men did not "lend to many nations" who "went about in sheepskins, in goatskins, being destitute, afflicted, ill-treated, wandering in deserts and mountains and caves and the holes of the earth", nor were they "blessed in city or in field"; but neither were their storehouses blessed, which they did not even possess in the first place. And consider whether from these things we shall not compel those who think otherwise to change their view (if they would preserve the dignity of God who gave the blessings) toward the position that he gave them spiritually to his own blessed ones.

Not only is every blessing with which Paul and those like him have been blessed spiritual, and none of them bodily, but it is also in the heavenly places. For it was fitting that these, whose "commonwealth exists in the heavens", who "lay up treasure in heaven" and have their "heart" where their treasure is, should also attain the spiritual blessings in the heavenly places. But it is worth examining how the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ has already blessed us with every spiritual blessing and in the heavenly places; for it is not said, 'who will bless' us. And consider whether in the heavenly places can stand for 'in the things perceived by the mind and beyond sense-perception'; for thus too one "lays up treasure" in "heaven", and no longer has his "heart" upon "earth", that is, among the material and bodily things, but in "heaven", ever conversing with the intelligible nature itself. And that we may consider it more precisely, both things are said concerning the blessing — both that it is spiritual and that it is in the heavenly places; and in addition to these that it is in Christ, that is, as it were, in the Word and the Wisdom and the Truth and the Power.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
But one might inquire, with regard to there being some who are holy and blameless before God, whether the prophetic word does not oppose this when it says "no living person shall be justified before you"; and if before God "every living person shall not be justified", how will there be some holy before him? For if they will be holy and blameless, they will also be justified.

One who takes refuge in the ambiguity of the prophetic saying will reply that the not-being-justified before God of every living person signifies something of this sort: that, as it were, wholly and out of the whole of his own lifetime "he shall not be justified" before God, in that he has certainly at some point sinned; and if this is so, it does not prevent there being some who are holy and blameless before him, having become such by correction; or else this too, that if not "every living person", yet at least some are justified.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
in love having predestined us unto adoption through Jesus Christ unto himself.

Either "in love" is to be joined with "having predestined", or thus: "he chose us in him in love before the foundation of the world, having predestined us" in adoption "through Jesus Christ unto himself, so that we should be holy and blameless before him".

The name of 'adoption' makes plain that those predestined by him are not by nature sons of God; the name of adoption, at any rate, could not be assigned to the Savior, but to those who, "having received" the "spirit" of "bondage" unto "fear", and "having rendered fear", become worthy of freedom and of hearing "you are no longer", I say, "servants", who also for this reason receive the "spirit" of "adoption". And when someone receives the Son, not having possessed him before, then the "spirit" of "adoption" has also come in; for thus through Christ adoption comes in upon us. Yet it is for the attaining unto himself that "he chose us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and blameless before him, in love having predestined us" in adoption "through Christ"; for to these words is appended "unto himself".

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
according to the good pleasure of his will.

The name of 'good pleasure' (εὐδοκία) is, I think, not very much worn into use in the customary speech of the Greeks, but was coined as a word by the translators; for they employed the term in the prophetic writings, as in the 84th [85th] psalm, "you were well pleased, O Lord, with your land", and in the 105th [106th], "remember us, O Lord, in the good pleasure of your people"; and in Habakkuk, "and if he draw back, my soul has no pleasure in him". But 'good pleasure' (εὐδοκία) exhibits within it the 'well' (εὖ) and the 'to seem fitting' (δοκεῖν); so that it would not be said of the things that seem to us not well, but only of those that seem so in a praiseworthy way.

One must therefore inquire how, in love having predestined unto adoption those whom God predestined, he predestined them according to the good pleasure of his will; and one must find the proof that there is a good pleasure of his will in these things; for indeed his will was well pleased in this, that the glory of his grace toward those who are being saved should be praised.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: The Saviour is called 'beloved' without qualification; for even if human beings go astray concerning the apprehension of "righteousness" and of "truth" and of "wisdom", nevertheless all would agree that they 'love' "wisdom" and "truth" and "righteousness". For this reason the Only-begotten of God is called 'beloved,' since all love the things conceived of him, whether they fall short of the mark or attain it — just as all stand in awe of God, but those who fall away from the sound conception concerning God go astray.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
A redemption is that by which release comes about for captives and for those who have fallen under their enemies; and we had fallen under our enemies, the "ruler of this age" and the evil powers under him, and for this reason we stood in need of redemption and of one to buy us back, so that, having been alienated from him, he might take us back. The Saviour therefore gave as the "ransom" on our behalf his own blood; wherefore we have the redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of trespasses.

Upon the redemption there follows the forgiveness of trespasses, since before anyone has been redeemed it is not possible for forgiveness of trespasses to come about for him. First, then, we must be redeemed and no longer be under the one who has taken us captive and prevailed over us, so that, having been set free and having come outside (so to speak) his hands, we may be able, for our benefit, to receive the forgiveness of trespasses, and, having been healed from the wounds of sin, to act according to piety and the rest of the virtues.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: He who has understood what "by grace you have been saved" means, and "not of works," and who "compares" trespasses with trespasses, would see — according to the parable that speaks of the "five hundred and fifty denarii" — who ought to confess greater thanks to the householder who remitted the debt. And further, observing how "the sufferings of the present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory that is to be revealed toward us," he would perceive the riches of the grace of God, and how it abounded thus toward the called and the elect, and most of all toward those who were "strangers to the covenants" of God and "aliens from" his "promises," who were drawn by the trespass of Israel, out of the fatherly kindness, to salvation; and still more would one grasp the riches of his grace, which he made to abound toward the blessed ones as something greater, observing the "do you not know that we shall judge angels?" and the "into which things angels long to look," and that which is said to be, at the end of all, "grant that, as I and you are one, they also may be one in us." And this whole riches of the grace of God, which he made to abound toward the saints, supplied from a certain beginning and increasing and being multiplied, whether vying in generosity in return and stretching itself out alongside so far as is possible, holds the one who attains the things spoken of before, or, where he falls short, so far as is possible does all the things that are incumbent. If, then, someone should fall short, the grace would become, as it were, void toward such a one; but if he should do without deficiency the things that lie with him, he would say the apostolic word, "his grace toward me was not made void."

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
What is in all wisdom and, after this, what is in prudence? Jesus too uses this expression in Wisdom, beginning from "all wisdom is from the Lord, and with him it is unto the age". If, then, someone has considered the things that are seen, and what are the things within them or even outside them that are not seen, and, dividing them off by reason — the invisible things by themselves and the visible things by themselves — should examine the wisdom by which God has made all things ("for you have made all things in wisdom", says David), such a one would be looking upon "all the wisdom that is from the Lord". But it is likely that someone, despairing that one still clothed about with this body can already come to be in all wisdom and prudence, and also giving heed to "we know in part and we prophesy in part", will take offense at in all wisdom and prudence having made known to us the mystery of his will, as being said by way of favor rather than truly; for granted that the mystery of God is made known in wisdom to Paul and to those like him, yet it is not in all wisdom that all things are made known to him who "knows in part and prophesies in part".

See, then, whether for this inquiry another division of the reading of the words in this passage is not fitting, running thus: unto the praise of the glory of his grace with which he graced us in the Beloved, in whom we have the redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of trespasses, according to the riches of his grace which he made to abound toward us in all wisdom and prudence; and here having brought to a stop the division of this passage, he will from another beginning read thus the words having made known to us the mystery of his will according to his good pleasure, so that in all wisdom and prudence is not attached to having made known to us the mystery of his will but to the words above. For God graced us in the Beloved in all his own wisdom and his own prudence; but also, having in the Beloved the redemption through the blood of Christ, we received these things in all the wisdom and prudence of God; and in all his wisdom and prudence we have obtained the forgiveness of trespasses, since he makes to abound toward us the riches of his grace in all wisdom and prudence; all of which things he has done, having made known to us the mystery of his will according to his good pleasure.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
But if the former reading also stands, an account such as this will be rendered, one not opposed to the working of "knowing in part" and of "pursuing so as to lay hold": in all his own wisdom and prudence God has dispensed us, having made known the mystery of his will. For in order that we may be able to know the mystery of his will and may have strength to make room for this, clothed about as we are with a "body of lowliness", we have need of all the wisdom of God dispensing us. And if the name of the mysteries is applied to things divine and unspeakable and not fit to reach unto the many, plainly it holds also concerning those who are to be saved by the will of the mystery of God; for the great multitude of the kindness of God is hidden for those who fear him, as David says, "how great is the multitude of your kindness, Lord, which you have hidden for those who fear you".

But attend to whether 'predestination' and 'purpose' differ, so that the purpose comes to be after the predestination; so that, as it were, according to the thoughts of God the predestination comes to be, while according to these same things the purpose concerning those whom he predestined follows upon the predestination — these being now, in a manner, given substance and coming into effect. Whence too it is written first, in love having predestined us unto adoption, and second, according to his good pleasure which he purposed in him.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But it must be examined what is the fullness of the times; and beside this lies the fullness of the time spoken by the same Paul, "but when the fullness of the time came, God sent forth his Son". And just as the time for the heir, having come to be at the stature of a man, to receive the paternal possession might in some way be named the fullness of his time or of his season, so a man would come to be in the fullness of the times who, through the ways and advancements that bear toward perfection, has arrived at being able to receive the things predestined and purposed by God for the saints.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
The word 'recapitulation' is used with reference to bankers and to the like, when accounts are reckoned up together and payments and expenditures or receipts are gathered into a single sum-total; hence, I think, the Apostle too has here made use of the expression. For, since there are many accounts of the administration of the things in the heavens and of the governance of the things upon the earth, all of them—inasmuch as they are parts of the one whole world—breathing together and inclining together toward a single result, there is a 'recapitulation' in Christ. For not only are the fragmentations of the things administered and the individual accounts of the things governed present in the Word of God and in his Wisdom, but also the recapitulation and (as one might say) the summing-up of all things.

Often 'sum-total' also means the comprehensive thought; at any rate it says, "a sum-total in what is being said," and "sum up many things in few." And 'sum-total' is so called, as I think, from the fact that our head too has everything in it, and all the sense-organs of our life, as it were in a sum-total.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Whatever God works and does and accomplishes, all these things he works according to the counsel of his own will; for there is nothing that can make him do anything contrary to the counsel of his will, since he is master over all things and rules over the universe. But in order that Paul might set forth the deliberateness of the workings of God that come to pass according to his will, he placed the counsel before the will. For beyond all others God does everything with counsel. Therefore he works all things according to the counsel of his will.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
In whom (that is, in Christ), besides others who have heard, you also, having heard the word of the truth—inasmuch as the gospel is a word of truth, of your salvation, in whom also, having believed, you were sealed with the Holy Spirit of the promise. Now it will seem, as regards the phrasing, that the second in whom is redundant, which has also been the cause of its seeming that, the thought being left hanging, the subordinate clause has not been supplied. But this is not so. Indeed one of those before us used to say that, out of his great love for Jesus, Paul very frequently makes mention of him and, as it were, superfluously, as one may see also in the case of in whom also, having believed, with respect to the in whom.

And it is entirely fitting for the Ephesians, who had shared in unspeakable words while Paul expounded them, to hear in whom you also, having heard the word of the truth. For I do not think that those who have heard only the preaching, and who have not received the accounts of the matters in narrative and clear unfolding, hear the word of the truth. For the word and the preaching differ, as Paul also teaches elsewhere, saying, "and my word and my preaching were not in persuasive words of wisdom but in demonstration of the Spirit and of power"; for there too it must be observed that he says his own word is something different from his own preaching. And it must be examined also whether in another epistle there stands the expression "that some have heard the word of the truth", so that the observation may appear more precisely according to Paul's intention.

But it must be observed where the term 'gospel' is named, and one must observe also the words that are added to it, such as "according to my gospel", or "the beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ", or "an eternal gospel", or the gospel of the salvation of the Ephesians; or simply 'gospel,' as when Paul says concerning Luke, "whose praise in the gospel is throughout all the churches".

And everyone who has heard the word of the truth—which is a gospel of the salvation of the one hearing and believing—is sealed with the Holy Spirit of the promise; so that if he should hear but not believe, he would not be sealed. But another will say that even if he should believe, yet not advance so far as to hear the word of the truth, not even so would he have room for the seal of the Holy Spirit of the promise, which is truly the impressing and clarifying of those things which it is fitting to be impressed and made clear by the Holy Spirit of the promise.

And it must also be inquired whether anywhere there is spoken of a holy spirit of promise, and what is to be understood by the Holy Spirit of the promise. I think, then, that just as the Holy Spirit, coming upon someone, makes him holy, and the "spirit of wisdom" makes him wise, and the "spirit of understanding" makes him understanding, so also the spirit of the promise makes one to be, in a way, already within the promise.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
You will inquire whether everyone who partakes of the Holy Spirit partakes of the spirit of the promise, or whether only the one who has heard the word of truth—which is a gospel of salvation—and has believed, this one receives the Holy Spirit of the promise; and further let us also fix our attention on this, whether everyone who in any way whatever partakes of the Holy Spirit has the pledge of the inheritance. But it is better to understand that, just as in the case of those who jointly purchase something and give a pledge, the pledge is given in proportion to the quantity of the whole sum of money, so too the pledge of the inheritance is given in proportion to the future goods foreknown for each saint, so that from the pledge one who is able to discern the differences of the power of one pledge and another might already be able to declare concerning the greater and lesser inheritance laid up for the fellow-heirs of Christ.

And just as the pledge of the inheritance is not something outside us (for in each one is the Holy Spirit of the promise, the pledge of the promise), so the inheritance is not outside the one who inherits, but in the mind of the one who inherits and in his soul; for nothing of external things can be compared with the perfection of a mind that beholds the beauties of the Wisdom and Word of God and of Truth.

This Holy Spirit of the promise, however, which is the pledge of our inheritance, is given to the saints in the present, so that they may be redeemed and made a possession for God, being made complete unto the praise of the glory of God.

And the phrase unto the praise of the glory of himself, in addition to the sense already rendered, can also indicate something of this kind: 'that each one exists for the praising of the glory of God, now receiving the spirit of the promise as a pledge of the inheritance, but later the inheritance itself;' not, however (as one might suppose to be signified from the wording), as though God had need of those who praise his glory, but rather as though the greatest goods accrue to those who have beheld the praiseworthiness of the glory of God and are not able to keep silent about it, but are ever engaged in rejoicing in the hymning of it.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: It will seem to be a solecism, the phrase "the eyes of the heart being enlightened in the knowledge of him", unless we render it as a hyperbaton; therefore we suppose that the sequence of the construction runs thus: "For this reason I also, having heard of the faith among you in the Lord Jesus, the eyes of your heart being enlightened in the knowledge of him, and that toward all the saints, do not cease giving thanks on your behalf, making mention of you in my prayers, that the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of glory, may give you a spirit of wisdom and revelation," unto your knowing what is the hope of your calling, and the rest.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: If the Father is father of something that subsists and is substantial, and he is called also the Father of glory, then plainly glory is something that subsists and is given substance; and perhaps our Savior, just as he is "the Word" and "Wisdom" and "Truth" and "Peace" and "Righteousness", so also is "Glory"; and if ever it is recorded that the "Glory" of God was seen, we must understand nothing else to have been seen than the Son of God.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Now the spirit of wisdom makes one wise, while the spirit of revelation takes away the veil from the heart, so that one, "with unveiled face beholding as in a mirror the glory of the Lord, is transformed into the same image from glory to glory". No one, then, who is not wise has a spirit of wisdom, and no one of those who still have, "whenever Moses is read, a veil upon the heart", has yet received the spirit of revelation; unless indeed the spirit of wisdom makes people wise in differing degrees according to the quantity of the contemplations of wisdom, and, according to the quantity of the removal of the veils that lie upon the letters, it administers the revelation not in like manner to those from whom the veil is removed.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: In addition to these things we must attend to the phrase "the eyes of the heart being enlightened in the knowledge of him"; for if knowledge of God and recognition of God are not the same, but the one who recognizes, as it were, knows again what he had known long ago and forgotten, then all who come into recognition of God knew him long ago; wherefore "all the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the Lord". And the phrase "the eyes of the heart being enlightened" discloses the incorporeal and intelligible nature of our ruling faculty and of "the true light".

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: The calling of God has a hope, which one must come to know from much attentiveness of life and readiness of mind; and his inheritance has a wealth of much glory in the saints, in the places above.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: He to whom, according to Paul's prayer, the spirit of wisdom and of revelation is given, that man will know the things "laid up" for those who are called, and will behold the things hoped for, which are the wealth of glory pertaining to his inheritance, which he gives to those who are called to this holy inheritance.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: You will inquire whether God himself too is the inheritance of the saints, so that the heirs of God are understood also in this sense, in order that, just as we speak of heirs of estates and heirs of houses, ranging the inheritance under the head of possessions, so we may understand also the heirs of God. And of just such a sense is the law that says "But to the sons of Levi you shall not give a portion in the midst of their brothers, for I am their portion, says the Lord," and elsewhere "The Lord is their inheritance."

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: The wealth of the glory of the inheritance of God, then, comes to be in the mind of the saints; since they will contain such great things of the contemplation of God and of his Word by the surpassing greatness of the power of God that is toward the saints and those who believe. For we have need not of some ordinary power from God for the knowing of what is the hope of his calling and what is the wealth of the glory of his inheritance in the saints, but of a greatness of his power coming to be in us who believe, coming from him, and coming according to the working of his strength that prevails over all things, which is now named by Paul the might of his strength; and it was by employing this working of the might of his strength that he wrought the things he wrought in Christ, when he raised him from the dead.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: We must hold that these things are said with a bodily figure, not as though there were certain perceptible seats or thrones set in the heavens, on which the Father sits, and the Son at the right hand of the Father; for if we understand them thus, we would not be speaking of these things worthily of the divine nature. For not even to God himself is "the earth" subjected in a bodily way, as he sits in heaven, as "the footstool of his feet". For how can "heaven be a throne", being measured by his span? And "the earth the footstool of his feet", when it too is enclosed within his fist? For Isaiah says, "Who measured the water with his hand, and heaven with a span, and all the earth with his fist?" I hold, therefore, that both being near to God and being far from him are matters of the mind, since all the saints, living according to the will of the Father of the universe and drawing near to God, are near, while the impious turn out to be far from him, concerning whom the prophet says, "Behold, those who remove themselves far from you shall perish". So then, just as it has been understood who is near to God and who is far from him, so we must hold that the saints are said to be at his right hand, and the impious as it were at his left, just as the Savior also says, "He will set the sheep at the right hand and the goats at the left". But indeed the phrase "having seated him at the right hand" is likewise of this sort: 'having established him and bestowed on him both a kingdom and a rule,' according to which he presides over and rules the saints, benefiting them and imparting himself to them—Jesus, who came to be far above all things through his benevolent dispensation toward all.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Many, then, are the things that rule and lead those who need his oversight, and many are the things that exercise authority, and many the things that exercise dominion, and many too the things that impart their own power, some being effective in this age, some also in the age to come; but none of these rules a rule as great as the Son does. For all the things that rule need him as their ruler; and indeed authorities will exercise authority better when they are under the authority of Christ, since the power of God surpasses all the rest of power; and even if someone is led into a profitable servitude by those who exercise dominion well, it is necessary that these things which exercise dominion, receiving the knowledge of how to exercise dominion from the "Lord of those who exercise dominion", exercise dominion over those over whom they do. Wherefore he who raised Christ from the dead seated him at his right hand in the heavenly places, far above every principality and authority and power and dominion, and every name that is named, not only in this age but also in the age to come; for it is likely that there are certain names, unspeakable and indescribable according to the ordering of the universe, not graspable by us, that are named—some in this age, but also some in the age to come. And whence come these names to the Apostle, except from the Holy Spirit that revealed them to him?

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: The One who is above all by definition has no one above him. He is not temporally following after the Father but eternally from the Father. This same thing is said of the Holy Spirit, according to the Wisdom of God, when it says "the Spirit of God has filled the world." If therefore the Son of God is said to be above all and the Holy Spirit is said to contain all, while God the Father is the one far above all names, it is plainly demonstrated that the nature and substance of the Trinity is one, which is above all.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But how it is said also that he subjected all things under his feet must be examined, since it is evident that there are countless multitudes who still do not submit to the Word of God. For "we do not yet see all things subjected"; and the saying "for he must reign until he puts all his enemies under his feet" makes clear that not yet are all the enemies under his feet. One person, then, will say that this too is said according to foreknowledge. But another, presenting the classification of God, by which he classes each into some rank, will say this: he subjected all things under his feet—as many as are of the rank of those who are subjected.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Finding the Church called the body of Christ, we inquire whether we must understand it, as the rest of the body in relation to the head, to be an instrument of the head; or whether, just as a man has a body, of which body the head is a part, so the whole Church of Christ is the body of Christ, animated by his divinity and filled by his Spirit; or whether these things must be taken in some other way. If, however, the second is the case, then the more human part of him will itself also be a part of the whole body, while the divine part, which gives life to the whole Church, will be the divine power that, as it were, animates it.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But how the Church, being the body of Christ, is the fullness of him who is filled, all in all, we wish to know, and why it is not said 'of him who fills all in all' but 'of him who is filled.' For it will seem more consistent to have said that Christ is the one who fills, and not the one who is filled; for he himself is the fullness not only "of the law", but is also the fullness of all fullnesses, since nothing becomes full apart from him. But see whether the one who speaks can respond to these things in this way: that, just as through the great relation and communion of the Son with rational beings the Son of God is, as it were, the fullness of all rational beings, so also he himself, as it were, takes up a fullness into himself, being shown to be most full in each of the blessed. And so that what is said may become clearer, consider a king who is filled with his kingship in each of those who increase the kingdom, but emptied of it in those who fall away; than this king nothing at all is more fitting to the benevolent kingdom of Christ, since each of those who together fill it is benefited by him rationally and made perfect—those who, fleeing to him for refuge, together fill up his body, which is somehow empty when it lacks those benefited. Therefore Christ is filled in all those who come to him, being deficient toward these until they come.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Clearly sins are said to be the death of the soul, from the phrase and you, being dead in your trespasses and your sins. And since 'trespass' is a term proper to Scripture, we must examine whether it differs from 'sin,' especially since here it is said in combination: and you, being dead in your trespasses and your sins. And we inquire whether the things already wickedly accomplished by us are called our 'sins,' while the beginnings of these—being, as it were, not yet falls, but on their way toward our actually falling—are 'trespasses.' And perhaps for this reason it is said in the eighteenth Psalm, "Who shall understand trespasses?", because the one who understands the roots and beginnings of sins, which are 'trespasses,' would be able also to guard himself against falling into 'sins' as well.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: The sequence is: And you, being dead in your trespasses and your sins, God made alive together with Christ, being rich in mercy through his great love with which he loved us; and being, us, dead in the trespasses, in which we once walked according to the age of this world, according to the ruler of the authority of the air, of the spirit that now works in the sons of disobedience, among whom we all also once conducted ourselves in the desires of our flesh, doing the wishes of the flesh and of the thoughts, and were by nature children of wrath—he made alive together with Christ. As for the connective of the passage, but God, being rich in mercy, we consider either to have been inserted pointlessly in the copies, or, as coming from Paul who was "unskilled in speech", not to have been perceived as superfluous.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: What is it to walk according to the age of this world, and not according to the age of the better world toward which the saints hasten? Now one person will, more simply, hold the age of this world to be the time coextensive with the constitution of this world from beginning to end. But another, from what follows, will suspect whether perhaps the ruler of the authority of the air, of the spirit that now works in the sons of disobedience, is the same as the age of this world, since all these things are set down as though of one entity, Paul saying, in which you once walked according to the age of this world, according to the ruler of the authority of the air, of the spirit; and in the letter to the Galatians he will think that the phrase "that he might deliver us out of the present evil age" shows that the "present age" is an "evil" living being, being the same as the ruler of the authority of the air, of the spirit (except that the saying from the letter to the Galatians admits of a counter-argument, since something similar is said also concerning days, which are agreed not to be ensouled: "buying up the time, because the days are evil," and "few and evil are the days that I have sojourned" upon the earth, says Jacob). And the passage "through whom he made the ages" will seem to call the ages a created thing, of which one is able to have become apostately "evil" and to be called the age of this world and the ruler of the authority of the air, of the spirit that now works in the sons of disobedience, among whom we all also once conducted ourselves.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: And it must be observed that he did not say 'according to the ruler of the air' but 'of the authority of the air'; therefore we must inquire into the authority of the air, that thus we may see the ruler of it. But the wording can also indicate something like this: according to the ruler of the authority, of the spirit—which spirit is the spirit of the air—that now works in the sons of disobedience. Since, then, the ruler is ruler of something, you will consider whether the one now spoken of is ruler of every authority concerning the air, which works, dwelling about the air, upon the sons of disobedience (and everyone who, when divine doctrines are proclaimed, disobeys them, by the very act of disobeying shows himself to be a son of disobedience); and consider whether "our wrestling" is against "these authorities", as we resist the workings which they wish to produce in us as well, wishing to make us sons of disobedience. And it is not to be wondered at that "these authorities" are said to be "in the heavenly places" (just as "the principalities and the authorities and the world-rulers in the heavenly places"), since the air about us is, according to a certain custom of Scripture, named 'heaven'; for it says "the birds of heaven", and it is clear that these are spoken of with reference to the air.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But the phrase and among whom we all also once conducted ourselves—among what things, if not the trespasses? For indeed he assigned nothing to correspond to the trespasses, but only to the sins; having said, at any rate, and you, being dead in your trespasses and your sins, he adds in which you once walked; but now he assigns, to correspond to your trespasses, the phrase and among which we all also once conducted ourselves, lest, having said in which you once walked according to the age of this world while keeping silent about himself, he should seem, as it were, to be boasting. But Paul himself knows a certain desire of the flesh, and another desire of the spirit, saying "the flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh".

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: And having conducted ourselves in the trespasses, since we were in the desires of our flesh, we did not one thing but many wishes, and not only of the flesh but also of the thoughts; and we inquire what the wishes of the thoughts are, being other than the wishes of the flesh; and we conjecture that, on the one hand, by doing the works of the flesh and loving pleasure one does the wishes of the flesh, while, on the other, by having fallen away from sound opinion and right thinking we do the wishes of the thoughts.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But as to the phrase we were by nature children of wrath, as also the rest, we do not know what those will ever say who introduce spiritual natures from the beginning; for how the one who is by nature Son of God is said to be by nature a son of wrath, let them answer. But we suppose that it was because of the "body of humiliation" that we became children by nature of wrath, when "our thought lay upon evil things from youth"; for according to Solomon, "there is no righteous person upon the earth who will do good and will not sin".

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: What Paul is saying then is: If you believe that Christ is risen from the dead, believe also that you too have risen with him. If you believe that he sits at the Father's right hand in heaven, believe that your place too is amid not earthly but heavenly things.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: As for he raised us up together and made us sit together: one who takes this in a more straightforward way will say that it is spoken according to the foreknowledge and predestination of God, as though what will be has already come to pass; but one who contemplates the kingdom of Christ as something perceptible only to the mind will not hesitate to say that the one who is already holy—just as he is not in the flesh even though he is said by the more straightforward to be in the flesh, so likewise he is not upon the earth even though, according to what is perceived by the senses, he is seen to be upon the earth. For the one who is in the spirit is not upon the earth, and none of those in the heavenly places is "in the flesh" but is already "in the spirit". Such dispositions, then, and the apprehension of things so great and of such a kind, is not earthly but heavenly, since all who already have "their citizenship in the heavens" have sat down together with Christ in the heavenly places, if indeed also "the kingdom of God is within us", so that in this way we may be seated in the heavenly places, sitting together with Christ and enthroned together with the Wisdom and the Word of God.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
Against those who suppose that those who have believed in Christ do not live by the commonwealth of Israel but by some other, new one that has nothing in common with that former one, a good observation may be taken from this passage. For *you were*, he says, *at that time without Christ, alienated from the commonwealth of Israel*, as though now they are no longer without Christ, nor indeed alienated from the commonwealth of Israel; for to all those who understand "the spiritual law" and live according to it, it belongs to be made at home in the commonwealth of Israel, and that more so than the bodily Jews; and it follows that the one who is without Christ and alienated from the commonwealth of Israel should also be reckoned a stranger to the covenants of the promise.

But you will inquire whether perhaps it is for this reason that it is said *without God in* this *world*; since, so far as concerns the foreknowledge of God, those to whom the epistle is written were not without God.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: The word *far off* and the word *near* were named from things that are spatially far or near, to set forth the disposition that is far from God and the one that draws near to His will; and we become *near* when we have been cleansed by the blood of Christ and "bought with this price".

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: It must be observed that, just as Christ is "word" and "wisdom" and "power" and "life", so too he is peace; and indeed one must gather together from all Scripture all the things by which he is named, so that we may understand him more accurately. Just as, then, the one who has him has the word, when he "sought and found" him as word (and the analogous holds also with respect to "wisdom" and "righteousness"), so let us seek him also as peace, in order that we may have him inasmuch as he is Peace and the peace of all rational beings; but the one who does not have peace does not have Christ.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: that these things are said concerning the more divine powers and those among men who are being saved — the more divine powers being near even before, but men being far off (and he who says these things will fit to them the "having made peace through the blood of his cross, whether the things upon the earth or the things in the heavens", and he will expound the whole passage in this way) — for the superior powers, that it was in friendship toward God, but for the men in the world, that it was in enmity toward him; and this enmity was the dividing wall of the partition, hindering the nature of men from being united to the blessedness of the superior ones. This dividing wall of the partition, then, being enmity, was broken down through our Savior's having become man, and for this reason it is said to have been broken down in his flesh.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
And attend indeed to what follows, whether it can be stated more strikingly by one who interprets in this way: according to the true law, of which "the letter was a shadow and a copy", namely that of Moses, certain ones "were serving" "in the heavenly places"; and that law is decrees rather than a law of commandments, which decrees the one who has been counted worthy to understand — by the breaking down of the dividing wall of the partition that walled him off from the superior ones — no longer lives by the law of the commandments; for Christ abolishes the law of the commandments in decrees, so that, once the decrees indicated by the law of the commandments have been understood, the law of the commandments may be despised as "the letter that kills".

The law of the commandments, therefore, having been abolished by the Savior through the manifestation of the decrees in them, brought together both — I mean the more divine powers and those among men who believe — into one new man. And the new man is understood from the "being renewed day by day", and he will be settled in a new world, because "there will be a new heaven and a new earth". But the [phrase] into one new man will seem to be contrary to the interpretation.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
In reference to what was said before, strangers to the covenants of the promise, it is now said so then you are no longer strangers and sojourners, and in reference to alienated from the commonwealth of Israel, there is now the [phrase] but fellow citizens of the saints and members of the household of God.

But these words must be brought to bear against those who introduce the [distinct] natures; for how are those who are by nature citizens of the saints strangers, and how are those who are by nature strangers members of the household of God?

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
And the earth was shaken and the rocks were split and the tombs were opened and many bodies of the saints who were sleeping rose again; and going out from the tombs after his resurrection they entered into the holy city and appeared to many (27, 51ᵇ—53).

And the earth was shaken, that is, all flesh, when the new word and new things according to the new covenant, and the new song, and all things new and heavenly came upon it, as the prophet too says in a certain place about this very thing: "all who saw them were confounded", that is, the disciples of Christ, "and every man feared". Likewise through another prophet the Lord says: "yet once more I will move the heaven and the earth and the sea and the dry land". But having said a little about the shaking of the earth, let us not unprofitably speak again also about the rocks split in the passion of the Lord the Savior, which were a mystery (as I think) of the prophets; for the law and the prophets were made manifest at the coming of Christ; and for this reason, when men "turn to the Lord" "while Moses is read, the veil which had been placed over their heart is taken away", and because "in the reading of the old covenant a veil had been placed, in Christ it is abolished". Now therefore the rocks have been opened and split, that we may see the spiritual mysteries placed in their depths. And we prove that the rocks then split are the prophets, first indeed from the fact that "Christ" is called the spiritual "rock", and it stands to reason that all imitators of Christ are likewise called rocks.

Just as they are also called "the light of the world" from the fact that their Lord himself is the "light" of the "world", and next from the fact that Peter too was called a rock by the Lord himself, when it is said to him: "you are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it". But this is shown most of all from the fact that all those against whom the "gates of hell" do not prevail, who have in themselves the work of the name of rock (that is, the apostles and the prophets) are themselves also rocks, and are the foundations of those who are built upon them, according to what the apostle says: "built up upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Jesus Christ our Lord himself being the highest cornerstone".

But those are built up upon the apostles and prophets most of all who are of the immaculate Church and who admire the apostles of Christ and do not despise the prophets, but examine also their scriptures.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
But the [words] from built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets will seem to agree with the interpretation concerning Israel's being near, but the nations far off.

And it will be necessary to use these texts against those who sever the Godhead and suppose that the prophets belong to one God and the apostles to another. For if those who are no longer strangers and sojourners but fellow citizens of the saints and members of the household of God are built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus himself being the cornerstone, in whom the whole building, fitted together, grows into a holy temple in the Lord, in whom the Ephesians also are built together into a dwelling place of God in the Spirit, then there is one God of one building and temple, which has been built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets. And if the whole building, fitted together, grows into a holy temple in the Lord, we must earnestly strive to become harmonious "living stones" for the whole building, so that, being built together, we may become a dwelling place for God, making room in ourselves for all his theology.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
As regards the phrasing, having sought so far as possible to set it in order, we say that he did not supply a corresponding clause to *For this reason I Paul, the prisoner*: what he did *for this reason*, or what happened to him, he did not really set forth—unless indeed, as regards the phrasing, he has fallen away from what should follow, "as one unskilled in speech," and has rendered the required sense not eloquently, whereas he would have said it thus: *For this reason I Paul, a prisoner of Christ Jesus and a prisoner for you Gentiles, made known the mystery* so as to impart it to you also, as I myself in the passages before this wrote in brief, *and you ought to have heard of the stewardship of the grace of God that was given to me for you who are of the Gentiles, for whose sake I have become a prisoner of Jesus Christ*. I think a solecism has occurred in this place; for whereas he ought to have said *For this reason I Paul, a prisoner of Jesus Christ, made known the mystery*, he instead says *For this reason I Paul, a prisoner, by revelation the mystery was made known to me*. But if anyone is able, alongside the sense, to show that the phrasing too was successfully managed by him, that person above all is to be heeded.

In the few passages before this, the one who reads carefully can truly find a revelation of a "holy mystery made known" to Paul.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: If our conscience "does not condemn us, we have boldness toward God." And it is a great thing not simply to have boldness, but boldness in confidence; and access as well, because of its sureness, again in boldness. And the beginning of the boldness in confidence and of the access is faith, the faith in Christ. And we have often said that he who does all things by reason has believed in Christ the Word, and he who grasps wisdom has believed in Christ the Wisdom, and he who declares the truth plainly has believed in Christ the Truth, and he who lives according to righteousness has believed in Christ the Righteousness.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
"Striving on behalf of" those being made disciples to Christ, he had many things that afflicted him; wherefore, he says, I ask that I not lose heart in my tribulations on your behalf; for to say these things belongs to one who perceives himself to be, as it were, in danger of losing heart.

After this we inquire to what we should apply the phrase which is your glory. One person, then, will say that he referred the which is your glory to the tribulations, as if he said 'which things are your glory,' but because 'glory' is singular—"being unskilled in speech"—he used the singular which instead of the plural 'which.' But another will refer the which is your glory either to the boldness or the access or the faith; for indeed the boldness is the glory of him who has it, and the access is the glory of him who is brought to God, and the faith might be said to be the glory of him who believes.

And the phrase wherefore I ask that I not lose heart in my tribulations on your behalf can be of this sort: 'wherefore I ask on your behalf, that you not lose heart in my tribulations, which are your glory.' And indeed what follows will seem to accord rather with this interpretation; for it is on this account that I bow my knees to the Father, that he may grant you, according to the riches of his glory, to be strengthened with power; for he who is not going to lose heart in tribulations needs to be strengthened with power.

But someone will say, against the second interpretation, that it made sense, when the Ephesians were being afflicted, for Paul to ask concerning them that they not lose heart, but it will seem ridiculous that, when Paul was being afflicted, the Ephesians should need prayer that they not lose heart in his tribulations. But against this one must set "your temptation which was in my flesh you did not despise nor spit upon"; for it is shown through these words that in the "flesh of Paul a temptation" came about for others. And in another way let us also consider whether this is not the very thing that most disturbs the many in discussions concerning providence, when they see countless tribulations and adversities befalling the most holy and most righteous, but the things reckoned good happening to the most lawless.

That Paul suffered many things in Ephesus and around Asia is written both in the Acts of the Apostles, and it is also possible to learn from him when he says "if after the manner of men I fought with beasts at Ephesus, what is the profit to me if the dead are not raised?"; and in the second epistle to the Corinthians, "For I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, concerning our affliction that came to pass in Asia, that we were weighed down exceedingly, according to our strength, so that we despaired even of living; but we ourselves have had within ourselves the sentence of death, that we should not be trusting in ourselves but in God who raises the dead, who delivered us from deaths so great and does deliver us, for we have hoped that he will also deliver us"; for see how many were his tribulations, so as to say "who delivered us from deaths so great and does deliver us".

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: The bowing of the knees is a symbol of another kneeling, which comes about in submitting oneself to God and in having fallen down before him. For it is by this reasoning that the Apostle too says "that in the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of things in heaven and things on earth and things under the earth", and we say that the heavenly beings do not altogether have bodies furnished with knees, and likewise too the beings under the earth, and in addition to these, neither do the souls that have been released from this body.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: He departed to his fathers. To what fathers? Those of whom Paul speaks: "Therefore I bow my knees before the Father, from whom every fatherhood receives its name."

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: His divinity seems, properly according to scripture, to be named his 'glory'. And God is rich in a divinity that is great and hard to grasp for created nature; imparting, then, from this riches of his divinity and glory to those to whom he judges it must be imparted—power and might—he strengthens with power through his Spirit; and he strengthens by settling Christ into the inner man that has room for him. And the most paradoxical thing: Christ, though he is whole and lives in himself, also dwells in those who partake of him; and he dwells through faith in the inner man, that is, in the governing faculty; for he adds, in your hearts.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
It seems to me that what follows is clearly stated in a solecism as regards the phrasing. For in relation to 'he would grant you' it would have been consistent to say 'to you rooted and grounded,' so that the sequence would be: that he may grant you, rooted and grounded in love, to be strengthened with power according to the riches of his glory through his Spirit, so that Christ may dwell in the inner man through faith; in the inner man, I mean according to your hearts, that is, the governing faculties.

But one who wishes to restore the passage without solecism—consider whether, having restored it thus, he will not do violence to the phrasing: For this cause I bow my knees unto the Father, from whom every family in heaven and on earth is named, that he may grant you according to the riches of his glory to be strengthened with power through his Spirit, that Christ may dwell in the inner man through faith, in your hearts, that, being rooted and grounded, you may be strong to comprehend with all the saints what is the breadth and length, and the rest. So that according to this interpretation the 'that' must be transferred from 'that you may be strong' to 'that, being rooted and grounded in love, you may be strong to comprehend.'

And in those rooted and grounded in the love toward God, namely "out of the whole soul and out of the whole heart and out of the whole strength and out of the whole mind", and in the love toward the "neighbour", Christ is settled. And as plants those rooted in love are rooted in it, so as a building they are grounded in love; and the same Paul said "you are God's tillage, God's building".

But it is a task to see in what sense the breadth is now spoken of, and in what sense the length, and in what sense the depth, and in what sense the height. Now the cross of Christ has all these, through which "having ascended on high he led captivity captive, and he descended into the lowest parts of the earth"—for it had both height and depth; and "into all the earth" he himself ran, reaching to its breadth and length. And he who is "crucified with" Christ and stretched out together with him comprehends the breadth and length and depth and height.

And it is also the task of the holy one to know the love of Christ which surpasses knowledge. And no one who has the love that surpasses knowledge can love any of the things that distract and drag him away from the comprehension concerning the knowledge that is surpassingly beloved.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
He keeps the unity of the Spirit who is "fitted together in the same mind and in the same judgment" of the Truth and of the Word and of the Wisdom toward his neighbor. But whenever we do not "all say the same thing," and for this reason "there are no divisions among us," we, not striving to keep the unity of the Spirit, break it up into many pieces. If indeed God gives "varieties of gifts," yet He keeps "the same Spirit"; and if He grants "varieties of ministries," yet He preserves "the same Lord"; and if He bestows "varieties of workings," yet "the same" remains "God who works all things in all."

To the Ephesians, therefore, who already possess the unity of the Spirit and need to keep it, it is said, in love striving to keep the unity of the Spirit; but to those who do not yet have the unity of the Spirit it would be said, 'striving to "attain to the unity" of the Spirit' or 'to do the things belonging to the unity of the Spirit.' And the unity of the Spirit is kept when love binds together those who are united according to the Spirit and gathers them into one body of Christ.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: On account of those who confound the Father and the Son, the word "Lord" is assigned to the Son, and "one God" to the Father; and against those from Valentinus who grant two baptisms, one must make use of the saying "one baptism".

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: He is "God and Father of all" in that of some he is "God" and not "Father", while of others he is "God and Father" — as if someone, pointing to ten men in number, of whom five are the sons of a certain man and five are slaves, were to say, "This man is lord and father of the ten."

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: It is impossible to speak of any parts or division in the incorporeal, but he is "in all and through all" … insofar as he is understood as either Wisdom or Word or life or truth, an interpretation which undoubtedly excludes all local confinement.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: In addition to these things one must examine the difference of the prepositions, of "over" and of "through" and of "in". And one may make use of a bodily image such as this: in place the sun is "over all", let us say, of the things upon the earth; but by its beams it might be said to be "through all"; and if the power of its light reached also into the depth of each thing, it would be said to be also "in all". So then, with respect to intelligible realities too, we think that his pre-eminence is indicated by "over all", his sufficiency toward each by "through all", while to reach also "in all" belongs to the power of "God", so that no one is wholly empty of him — this by "in all".

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: And "to each one of us was given grace according to the measure of the gift of Christ" we suppose to have been understood thus. "God does not give the Spirit and grace by measure, he whose majesty has no limit"; but he gives a "measure" out of sparing consideration for those who receive, since each one has no room for more than what he receives to his benefit. Yet since it is grace that is given — and "it is not of works, since grace would no longer be grace" — the grace is given according to the measure of the gift of Christ; and even if not "of works", still it depends on something at least that is in our power. For the grace is given "of faith", so that, the grace cooperating, faith may be adorned also with works, so that the one who receives the grace may say, "and his grace toward me was not in vain, but I labored so much".

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: If, on the other hand, as it reads in some manuscripts, "even in those who did not sin in the likeness of Adam's transgression," this death, namely that which was keeping souls bound in the underworld, is said to exercise dominion, then we shall understand it to mean that even the saints had fallen prey to that death certainly under the law of dying, even if not under the punishment of sin. But it was on this account that Christ descended into the underworld, not only because he would not be held by death [Acts 2:24], but also in order that he might release those who were held there, as we said, not so much through the crime of transgression as much as by the condition of dying. As it is written, "Many bodies of saints who were sleeping were resurrected with him and entered into the holy city." [Matthew 27:52-53] In this as well the prophet's sayings were fulfilled, in which he said of Christ, "In ascending on high he led captivity captive." [Ephesians 4:8-9] Thus by his own resurrection he has already destroyed the dominions of death, which is also why it is written that he set captivity free.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
In connection with what precedes, he brings in these things too. For if Christ is "over all and through all and in all", yet to each of the saints was given grace according to the measure of the gift of Christ, so that some are apostles, some prophets, and others evangelists, and after these pastors, and over all teachers.

If, therefore, to be a "teacher" is a gift given "according to the measure of the gift of Christ", then clearly a "pastor" also who shepherds with knowledge must shepherd as one having a gift. And how will anyone be an "evangelist" whose "feet" of the soul are not, so to speak, beautiful? And for them to become so, God must furnish them with beauty. But so too a "prophet" "who reproves and examines the unbelieving" (for such is the "prophet" of the new covenant), whom one must consider to be appointed for the Church by "God". And if it is possible for these to be always in the Church, perhaps also "apostles", to whom it is given "to work the signs of the apostle", may possibly be found even now.

And there is need of "apostles and prophets" and the rest "for the perfecting of the saints", that they may be perfected "according to the work of the ministry of Christ", so that "the body of Christ may be built up and made to function" out of the "living stones".

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Two ages are spoken of in the Scriptures: one of the body, which is not in our power but in the law of nature; the other of the soul, which properly lies within us, and according to which, if we will, we daily grow and come to its summit, "so that we may be no longer little children, tossed about and carried around by every wind of doctrine", but, ceasing to be "little children", may begin to be "men" and may say: "when I became a man, I destroyed the things that belonged to a little child". Of this age, as I said, the advancement, which is the increase of the soul, is in our power. But if this testimony is not enough, let us take yet another example from Paul: "until we all attain", he says, "to a perfect man, to the measure of the age of the fullness of the body of Christ". It is in us, therefore, that we should "attain to the measure of the age of the body of Christ"; and, if it is in us, let us strive with all effort to lay aside the little child and to destroy him and to come to the remaining ages.
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 20

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
One must inquire who the "all" are who "shall attain to the unity of the faith" — whether "all" men without qualification, or we who have been allotted our portion in Christ. It will seem to have been assigned to the former, because there are many winds of teaching that toss and carry about, in the sleight of men, in craftiness aimed at the scheming of error, well-nigh all men, or the most of them.

Yet one must strive earnestly to attain "to the unity of the faith", and, in addition "to the unity of the faith", to come to be also "in the unity of the knowledge of the Son of God".
